HEADLINE: Victoria police trial virus saliva tests in pilot program
TEXT:
More than a thousand Victorian police officers are involved in a trial of a saliva test for COVID-19 that could speed up the detection process in high-risk workplaces.

So far, two have tested positive. The pilot program is being rolled out over two weeks at three police stations in Melbourne and the regional towns of Bendigo and Dandenong. It uses a test proven effective by the Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity.

Saliva tests for COVID-19 are being used around the world, but this pilot is novel because it uses pooled samples. This means a few samples are tested together instead of individually. In this case, four.

If the pool tests negative, there is no need to test the individuals. If the pool tests positive, each person is tested. This makes the testing process faster and more efficient. Pooling is a standard technique used by blood banks to check the safety of blood donations.

"We believe we are the first to pilot pooled testing of saliva samples for effective and user-friendly workplace surveillance," said Mike Catton, Doherty's deputy director who is leading the pilot.

"While only in the first stage of the pilot, we have identified the preferred method of collecting the saliva and have diagnosed two cases of COVID-19 among the participants.

"This is a good indication of proof of concept and highlights the importance of higher-risk workplace testing as a surveillance method,"

Dr Catton, who is also director of the Victorian Infectious Diseases Reference Laboratory, is optimistic the pilot will provide a clear picture of whether this approach is a feasible solution in higher-risk settings.

"Saliva testing has been trialled in the Doherty Institute public health laboratories and in labs around the world and while the nasal swab remains the gold standard of COVID-19 testing, this could be an excellent alternative in some settings," he said. As an alternative to a nasal swab, the test has been validated by the Doherty and proved highly accurate.

He says there is clearly potential for self-collection of saliva and this may be a better option in the future.

The pilot is a partnership between the Victorian government and Doherty, and the first phase uses different methods of saliva collection to determine which is the most effective and comfortable way to mass test in a workplace setting.

The three methods are mouth to container, a swab under the tongue and mouth to straw to tube.

The next phase will test a greater number of workers in other higher-risk workplace settings. "I think this is an important study. It's been agreed nationally by the Public Health Laboratory Network and we all support it," said Professor Bill Rawlinson, a senior medical virologist at UNSW Sydney.

The sensitivity and specificity of saliva tests are as good as swab tests, he said.

The attraction is that they are low-cost and reduce the risk to healthcare workers if they do not need to collect the sample.

They also overcome the reluctance of some to have nasal or throat swabs. The tests may better suit young children, people with disabilities and the elderly who may have conditions that render them anxious or confused.

HEADLINE: Border opening gets SA tourism tills ringing
TEXT:
Call it the border tipping point. When South Australia's Premier Steven Marshall announced he would fully reopen his state to NSW as of 12.01am on Thursday, September 24, the flow-on effect was dramatic.

Even Prime Minister Scott Morrison took advantage, flying from Sydney to Adelaide aboard his VIP jet on Friday, ahead of Saturday's annual general meeting of the South Australian Liberal Party, where he will reiterate the economic and community benefits of opening borders.

The proof is already there: Flight Centre's online bookings for flights from NSW to SA jumped 250 per cent within hours of Mr Marshall's September 22 announcement, with Qantas and Virgin reporting Sydney-Adelaide and vice versa quickly shot to the top of the nation's most booked domestic routes.

Room bookings across South Australia rose by 28 per cent for AccorHotels, and the Google search "things to do in SA" surged by 200 per cent.

"We're heartened by this, but the real boost will come when Queensland reopens," Flight Centre boss, Graham "Skroo" Turner, told AFR Weekend.

"And Western Australia - all the borders should be open, even Victoria. We need borders open well before Christmas to get the economy moving."

AccorHotels chief operating officer for the Pacific region, Simon McGrath, agreed, pointing out while bookings were generally picking up, "Christmas remains subdued, which we are linking to ongoing feelings of uncertainty. As witnessed in South Australia, the minute there's certainty around a border, business kicks in."

AccorHotels' regional occupancy rates are now running at about 40 per cent, peaking to 75 per cent in busy periods such as school holidays. Half of the chain's 21,000-strong workforce are back at work, with the rest still on JobKeeper.

"We're getting there, but it's still a long way from our 85 per cent occupancy average pre-COVID," Mr McGrath said. "There's a tough road to walk yet."

Prime Minister Scott Morrison has felt the constraint. Apart from a brief foray to Queensland in July - which was cut short due to the Victorian outbreak - Mr Morrison's Adelaide trip will be the first time he has travelled outside of NSW or the ACT in about three months.

"What better way to celebrate our borders being open for business to NSW - not only can we now welcome back hundreds of tourists and see families reunited, we also get to showcase Adelaide to the Prime Minister," South Australian Tourism Commission chief executive Rodney Harrex said.

"The border reopening to our second-biggest domestic market [behind Victoria] is already proving to be the shot in the arm we needed," Mr Harrex said. "Operators across the state are already reporting an influx of bookings from NSW for the school holidays."

It will be a while before South Australia recovers its pre-COVID-19 record $8.1 billion visitor economy of 2019.

But the green shoots are now sprouting, especially given one in four domestic visitors to the state is from NSW, with NSW travellers spending about $779 million in SA each year.

It was welcome news to the state's thousands of tourism businesses, such as the Deviation Road Cellar Door in the Adelaide Hills. Despite a few days of cold weather, not much could dampen the mood of the winery's owners, Hamish and Kate Laurie, on Friday.

"We've been fielding a lot more inquiries over the past few days, and more people are turning up during the week, it's not mainly weekend trade," Mr Laurie said on Friday.

"We've done a lot of intrastate trade the past month or so, given no one can go overseas. But the 50 or so cellar doors in the Adelaide Hills are very dependent on interstate trade; that's a big market for us, so we're looking forward to welcoming travellers from NSW."

South Australia's tourism spike is yet more good news on the back of the other great litmus test for the local industry: when a seven-hour Qantas joy-ride flight to nowhere sold out in 10 minutes on September 17.

About 150 tickets on the October 10 flight, priced from $787 to $3787, were snapped up almost immediately, making global headlines.

WITH PHILLIP COOREY

It's already proving to be the shot in the arm we needed. Rodney Harrex, SA Tourism Commission

HEADLINE: NSW denies it is copying Victoria's contact tracing system
TEXT:
The Berejiklian government has denied a claim by Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews that NSW is adopting a new technology platform used by its southern neighbour for contact tracing.

The Victorian government has deployed a cloud-based system developed by Salesforce in an attempt to accelerate contact tracing. This came after officials admitted the state's contact tracers were overwhelmed at the peak of the second wave.

Asked on Sunday about a visit by Victorian officials to Sydney to review the NSW contact tracing system, Mr Andrews said: "I'm happy to confirm for you that the biggest outcome out of that is that NSW will be copying our IT platform.

"The biggest discussion at the national cabinet meeting was that the CRM [customer relationship system] package we will put in place we will work really hard with NSW to make sure they have the same system. So they will take the system that we have and try to run it up there, which I think is fantastic."

But the NSW government has denied Mr Andrews' claim.

"At this stage NSW Health has no plans to adopt the Victorian IT platform for contact tracing," a NSW Health spokeswoman said in a statement.

The spokeswoman said the Department of Health was "continuing to exchange information with and learn from all states and territories".

"NSW Health has well-established processes and systems for managing people with notifiable infectious diseases and their contacts. This includes infectious diseases such as measles, tuberculosis, and HIV as well as COVID-19.

"The NSW contact tracing team has the capacity to rapidly scale up when case numbers increase."

The Salesforce system is being used by Western Australia, South Australia, New Zealand and 35 US states. Victoria is also planning to use IBM's cognitive intelligence program, Watson, to search for patterns in cases that could aid future tracing.

The denial comes after Mr Andrews angrily pushed back on a call by Prime Minister Scott Morrison, Treasurer Josh Frydenberg and Health Minister Greg Hunt on Sunday calling for an earlier easing of restrictions.

"We note that at similar case levels, NSW was fundamentally open while remaining COVID-safe due to a world class contact tracing facility," they said.

"I saw the Prime Minister's statement yesterday. He can speak to that, he can speak to why, for instance, he thinks that's the most productive thing to do," Mr Andrews said.

"I don't issue statements like that. I'm more focused on getting the job done. I'm not interested in a quarrel with the Prime Minister."

HEADLINE: WA budges on border, active cases decline
TEXT:
Western Australia has recognised the dramatic improvement in COVID-19 infections in the eastern seaboard states, lifting bans on travellers from NSW and Victoria, and maintaining a mandatory 14-day home quarantine rule.

All interstate travellers will still be required to apply for permission to travel to Western Australia. Victorians will be subject to tighter entry requirements and will have to take a COVID-19 test on arrival in Perth and again on day 11 of their quarantine.

Premier Mark McGowan said people coming to WA should download a new "G2G Now" app.

This will use face recognition and location data to allow police to check on people remotely while in self-quarantine. A similar app is in use in WA and Tasmania to manage permitted travel within the state.

Mr McGowan said the app would free up police resources and enable the state to increase international arrivals.

Nationally, there were 19 new cases reported.

The first relaxation of Australia's toughest border controls came after Victoria recorded 9 new cases.

The number of active cases have fallen to 326, a third of the level compared with a fortnight ago. A further seven people died from COVID-19, and six of these deaths were associated with aged care homes.

The state average for the past 14 days is at 18.2 cases and mystery cases without a known source have fallen by 4 to 27.

The next phase of relaxations can occur when the statewide 14-day average drops below 5 cases and there are fewer than 5 cases with an unknown source over the previous fortnight. NSW had its fourth day in a row without a single locally-acquired case of COVID-19; two cases were reported from hotel quarantine.

Western Australia was the only other state to report new cases, with an additional 8 cases added from a bulk ore carrier moored near Port Hedland. This brought the total confirmed cases associated with the ship to 17. Seven are aboard the ship as part of the essential crew and 10 in hotel quarantine.

Mr McGowan said infected sailors were being kept under tight supervision and the Australian Defence Force and the Australian Maritime Safety Board were assisting.

Port Hedland is the biggest port for Australia's most lucrative export commodity, iron ore - BHP, Fortescue Metals, Roy Hill and Mineral Resources Limited ship their product through this port.

The WA government agency in charge of Port Hedland, the Pilbara Ports Authority, said those miners were not being affected by the confirmed cases of the virus in the port.

"There have been no impacts to our port operations," a spokeswoman said yesterday.

WA Health Minister Roger Cook said the world's leading expert in vessel management was helping out and the infection control team had done similar work on a larger scale with the Artania cruise ship in Fremantle in April.

Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews said all outstanding cases had been notified and interviewed, and claimed that 80 per cent of interviews had occurred in the first four hours and that all close contacts had been completed within the 48-hour period.

"We've seen obviously when you're not overwhelmed by literally thousands of cases, then this contact tracing team, like any contact tracing team across the world, are in a position to respond even more quickly and that's exactly what they're doing," Mr Andrews said.

Key pointsInterstate travellers will still be required to apply for permission to travel to WA.

Victoria records nine new cases and the number of active cases falls to 326.

HEADLINE: Top 200 write down $32b because of COVID-19
TEXT:
Top 200 companies have written more than $32 billion off their balance sheets, mostly attributed to COVID-19, says an EY analysis of last year's financial results, but CEOs are relatively optimistic the country can achieve growth in the next three years.

Yesterday, Bank of Queensland was the latest, booking a $175 million provision for souring loans. The big banks wrote off almost $12 billion, followed by commercial property groups like Scentre, GPT and Vicinity which wrote off more than $10 billion. Qantas also had a $1.4 billion write-down.

The EY analysis, however, suggests the largest companies have responded with an almost equal amount of capital raisings in the same period - $26.5 billion - putting them in a decent position to rebound into a growth phase.

KPMG's annual CEO outlook survey shows top chief executives are relatively optimistic about their three-year growth outlook - 74 per cent of Australian CEOs are confident about the earnings outlook, a relatively modest slip from 86 per cent at the start of the year.

Over 50 per cent of the CEOs expect growth of between zero and 2.5 per cent in the next three years, while 30 per cent expect growth of 2.5 per cent to 5 per cent; 16 per cent predict no growth or falling revenue.

The CEOs are most optimistic about their own business but less positive about their own industry and even less so about the broader domestic and global economy. Only 42 per cent are relatively optimistic about the prospects for their country and only one-third of local CEOs hopeful about the world economy.

"Australia CEOs do seem a little more optimistic than their global counterparts," said KPMG Australia chief executive Gary Wingrove.

"In general, bigger businesses have weathered this ok, I think it's smaller businesses who are struggling and have been hit harder than bigger business. The fact we've had less insolvencies than 12 months ago doesn't seem right ... there will be a time of reckoning, it's a question of whether the government can somehow smooth that to assist as many as possible to the other side." On the $32 billion reported in write-downs, EY's M&A partner Duncan Hogg said most of the equity raisings were taken early on with the highest proportion in April.

While he doesn't expect another wave of capital raisings, both financial services and real estate had far bigger write-downs than their raisings, leaving them most susceptible to a shortage of cash. "In our view, companies will now favour raisings for growth rather than survival," he said.

"If there were to be further raisings to reinforce balance sheets, it is most likely these will occur in the financial services and real estate sectors."

The KPMG CEO survey of 1300 CEOs across the globe in January-February, supplemented by a second survey of 315 leaders in July-August (including 50 from Australia), showed talent and supply chain risks have climbed the list of CEOs' top risks. Respondents reported that digital strategies had been accelerated by several years.

The coronavirus pandemic has also hit CEOs personally. Forty per cent said a member of their extended family had health affected by COVID-19, 70 per cent in Australia and internationally said their personal experience had reshaped their strategy and half of Australian CEOs and 63 per cent globally said they took a pay cut.

HEADLINE: Universities in line to receive an extra $1b
TEXT:
The federal government will inject more than $1 billion into higher education in next week's budget for new student places and research, but it is unlikely universities will get the multibillion-dollar research bailout they are looking for, because of the soaring budget deficit.

Education Minister Dan Tehan will tell the The Australian Financial Review Higher Education Summit in Sydney today there will be an extra $326 million in the budget for new university places, the equivalent of 12,000 new students.

That brings to 30,000 the number of additional places proposed under the Jobs-ready Graduates package.

Mr Tehan says the government is aware of the need to support falling research budgets and was working with vice-chancellors on a sustainable support package.

It is understood the budget will provide $750 million in immediate relief. This falls short of the estimated $1.5 billion in research money that has been lost this year as the international student market collapsed.

Mr Tehan will tell the Summit that Australia needs to get better at commercialising its research and at turning ideas into jobs, productivity and growth. This will involve centres of excellence where more than one university works on a project, sharing costs and benefits. Some good examples were working even at a small scale.

"For example, our government is investing $2 million in the Nowra Agri-business Innovation Hub to connect the regional agribusiness sector with the latest technologies and research," Mr Tehan will say. "We are providing a further $2 million for a pilot program to teach shipbuilders digital skills to take on high-tech jobs at the Osborne naval yard in South Australia."

The government recognises the role university research plays in COVID-19 and that it would underpin economic recovery after the pandemic.

He was looking at options proposed by the Research Sustainability Working Group that is working for a long-term model of funding that is not vulnerable to international student income. He wanted an outcome that was "good at working with industry and in commercialising research".

The $750 million will allow researchers to finish existing work, but leaves a question mark over long-term research, with the Centre for the Study of Higher Education at Melbourne University tipping the shortfall in research funding will hit $7.6 billion by 2024.

Mr Tehan describes the pandemic and Jobs-ready Graduates Package as reshaping the architecture of higher education and says as a consequence universities "will focus on domestic students like never before".

"The Morrison government wants more Australians to undertake a degree, learn a trade, study a vocational qualification, upskill with a micro credential, start a business or get a job."

A special transition fund will be set up as the JRG package is introduced to "lock in indexation" and give certainty to universities. Universities have complained the net effect of the bill is a 6 per cent fall in income from domestic students.

In line with this, a change was possible in the way performance funding money will be increased.

An undisclosed amount will be invested in short-term courses, which is part of a plan to create "stackable" qualifications. Since the crisis the government had funded 400 short courses.

"The development of micro-credentials will drive innovation and provide an additional income stream for universities, while making them more efficient, relevant to industry and responsive to the requirements of domestic students.

"We want to create new business opportunities for education providers by cutting red tape and allowing international students to study micro-credentials in areas outside their primary course of study."

This would involve a bigger focus on regional Australia and he wants to overturn the "discrepancy" where young people in regional areas are half as likely to obtain a university qualification as young people who live in the city.

On international students, he says Darwin is about to start a pilot program to bring in 70 overseas students.
